Series::i0¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::i0() const
Series& Series::i0_()

What It Does¶

Computes the modified Bessel function of the first kind, order zero, I0, elementwise:

I0(x) = sum_{k>=0} (x/2)^(2k) / (k!)^2

I0 is the normalizing constant of the von Mises distribution — the circular analogue of a Gaussian — so i0() shows up whenever a density or likelihood is defined over angles. It is also the shape factor of a Kaiser window and appears in the amplitude statistics of narrowband noise (the Rician distribution).

Behaviour:

  • I0(0) = 1, its minimum.

  • I0 is even: I0(-x) = I0(x).

  • It grows very fast — roughly e^|x| / sqrt(2 pi |x|) for large |x| — so i0() overflows float64 for |x| past about 713.

  • It is smooth and strictly positive everywhere; there are no poles or branch points.

i0() is out-of-place; i0_() overwrites the current storage.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series or Series& A Series with the same shape as self, each element replaced by I0(x). i0_() returns a reference to the mutated series.

An integral input is promoted to float64.

Gradient¶

i0() is differentiable everywhere. Its derivative is the order-one modified Bessel function I1:

d/dx I0(x) = I1(x)

I1 is odd and I1(0) = 0, so a tracked i0() has zero slope at the origin and a slope that grows with |x| away from it. The backward pass evaluates I1 directly.

Examples¶

Example 1. I0 rises from 1 at the origin.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0}).i0()
) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 1.2661, 2.2796, 4.8808]

Example 2. I0 is even.

pluss::series::print(std::cout,
                     pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 1.0, 3.0}).i0());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[4.8808, 1.2661, 1.2661, 4.8808]

Example 3. The backward pass is I1(x). Although the forward function is even, its derivative must be odd: equal-magnitude negative and positive inputs produce opposite sensitivities.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.i0().sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.5906, -0.5652, 0.0000, 0.5652, 1.5906]

Example 4. Integral inputs are promoted to float64.

pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({0, 1, 2}).i0());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 1.2661, 2.2796]

Example 5. i0_() overwrites the current storage in place.

auto a = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 2.0});
a.i0_();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a);

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 1.2661, 2.2796]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • I0 grows exponentially. For |x| past roughly 713 the result overflows to +inf. When you only need a ratio or a log — a von Mises log-likelihood, for instance — rescale before calling rather than dividing two large I0 values.

  • This is the modified Bessel function I0, not the oscillatory J0. I0 is monotone on [0, inf) and never negative.

  • The gradient is I1, not I0 itself.

  • Integral inputs promote to float64.

  • i0_() requires floating storage. An integral receiver cannot represent the non-integral result, so use the out-of-place i0() to obtain float64.

Summary¶

i0() is the order-zero modified Bessel function I0:

  • I0(0) = 1, even, strictly positive, no singularities

  • grows like e^|x| / sqrt(2 pi |x|); overflows for |x| past ~713

  • differentiable everywhere with backward I1(x)

  • i0_() is the in-place form

See Also¶

  • Series::sinc: another smooth entire special function.

  • Series::lgamma: a log-space form for a function that otherwise overflows, the same trick I0 ratios need.
